title: DEEPANSHU BANSAL versus POONAM BHATT   Advocate- ,SOUBHAGYA RANJAN PATI 1123

paras.text:
UKHC010159552026
HIGH COURT OF UTTARAKHAND AT NAINITAL
Appeal From Order No.332 of 2026
Deepanshu Bansal .............Appellant
Versus
Poonam Bhatt ...........Respondents
Present:- Mr. Arvind Vashistha, Senior Advocate assisted by Mr. Ajeet Kumar
 Yadav Advocate and Ms. Sneha Sethia, Advocate holding brief of Mr.
 Vikas Khera, Advocate for the appellant.
Mr. Soubhagya Ranjan Pati and Mr. Chandra Prakash, Advocate for
the Caveator/respondent.
JUDGMENT
Hon'ble Ravindra Maithani, J. (Oral)
The challenge in this appeal is made to order dated
18.07.2026, passed in Civil Suit No.01 of 2024, Deepanshu Bansal
Vs. Poonam Bhatt, by the court of First Additional District Judge,
Udham Singh Nagar ("the suit"), by which an application filed
under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 read with Section 151 of the Code of
Civil Procedure, 1908 ("the Code"), filed by the appellant has been
dismissed.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the
record.
3. Facts necessary to appreciate the controversy, briefly
stated, are as follows. The appellant filed the suit under Sections
134 and 135 read with Sections 27(2) and 29 of the Trade Marks
Act, 1999 ("the Act") for permanent injunction restraining
infringement and passing off of trademarks, rendition of accounts,
etc. It is the case of the appellant that they are into the business of
marketing and trading of gold, silver, diamond, platinum and other

2
jewelleries. On 09.09.2022, they applied for registration of the trade
mark "SUNAREKA", which was finally granted to them on
28.07.2023 and in view of Section 23 of the Act, it relates back to
the date when the application was made for registration of
trademarks. The appellant provides 100% hallmark jewelleries and
precious metals to their customers. The trademark granted to the
appellant has already become distinct and associated with the
appellant.
4. It is the case of the appellant that the respondent
substantially copied the registered and well known
trademarks/label of the appellant. The respondent is also engaged
in the business of marketing and trading of gold, silver and its
jewelleries. She started using the trademark "SWARNIKA" and
thereby they are confusing consumers in each and every respect
including visually, structurally, in its basic ideas and essential
features. The respondent has substantially copied the registered
and well known trade mark/label of the appellant. According to the
appellant, the imitation is in exactitude of copying in such manner
that not only ordinary purchaser but also the big
retailers/dealers/distributors are bound to be confused/deceived.
With these and other averments, appellant seeks permanent
injunction restraining the respondent from using the trade
mark/label or any other trade mark respectably similar to the
appellant's trademark "SUNAREKA".
5. The respondent did file her Written Statement and
according to her , the trade mark/label/brand name "SWARNIKA
Gems and Jewels", is derived from the word, "Swarn" which in itself

3
is a meaning of gold. The respondent stated that she had also filed
an application for registration of the trade mark on 05.06.2023,
which is yet to be processed. According to the respondent, the trade
mark, "Swarnika Gems and Jewels" is totally distinct and different
from any other trade marks/brand name. The main element of
respondent trademark is "SWARNIKA", which is coined and
inspired from the word "Swarn". With these and other averments,
the respondent claims that the suit filed by the appellant be
dismissed.
6. In the suit, an application under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2
and 151 of the Code was filed by the appellant, which has been
rejected by the impugned order. It is impugned herein.
7. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant
submits that the appellant has a registered trade mark in the name
of "SUNAREKA" and it is being infringed by the respondent by
running her business in the name of "SWARNIKA" which is
deceptively similar. It is argued that the articles that are being sold
by both the appellant and the respondent are similar and identical.
They are dealing with jewelleries.
8. Learned Senior Counsel would also submit that in the
impugned order, the court has discussed the two words
"SUNAREKA" and "SWARNIKA" and considered that the spellings
are different. It is argued that there cannot be a dissection. The
words as a whole and in totality are to be seen. In support of his
arguments, learned Senior Counsel placed reliance on the principle
of law as laid down in the case of Under Armour Inc Vs. Anish

4
Agarwal and another, 2025 SCC OnLine Del 3784. In the case of
Under Armour Inc (Supra), the Hon'ble Delhi High Court has
discussed the concept of anti-dissection rule and in para 43
observed as follows:-
"43. It is well settled that the question
whether competing trademarks are similar cannot
be decided by dissecting them and then comparing
their parts for similarities. In South India Beverages
India Private Limited v. General Mills Marketing Inc.;
2014 SCC OnLine Del 1953: a Division Bench of this
court had observed "conflicting composite marks are
to be compared by looking at them as a whole, rather
than breaking the marks up to their components
parts for comparison"."
9. Further in the case of Under Armour Inc (Supra), Hon'ble
Delhi High Court also referred the text from McCarthy on
Trademarks and Unfair Competition, and in para 47 observed as
follows:-
"47. We consider it apposite to refer to the
following text from McCarthy on Trademarks and
Unfair Competition, which explains the said
principle as under:-
"23.15 Comparing Marks : Differences v.
Similarities
[1] The Anti-Dissection Rule
[a] Compare composites as a Whole :
Conflicting composite marks are to be compared by
looking at them as a whole, rather than breaking
the marks up into their component parts for
comparison. This is the "anti dissection" rule. The
rationale for the rule is that the commercial
impression of a composite trademark on an
ordinary prospective buyer is created by the mark
as a whole, not by its component parts. However, it
is not a violation of the anti-dissection rule to view
the component parts of conflicting composite marks

5
as a preliminary step on the way to an ultimate
determination of probable customer reaction to the
conflicting composites as a whole. Thus, conflicting
marks must be compared in their entireties. A mark
should not be dissected or split up into its
component parts and each part then compared with
corresponding parts of the conflicting mark to
determine the likelihood of confusion. It is the
impression that the mark as a whole creates on the
average reasonably prudent buyer and not the parts
thereof, that is important. As the Supreme Court
observed:"The commercial impression of a
trademark is derived from it as a whole, not from its
elements separated and considered in detail. For
this reason it should be considered in its entirety."
The anti-dissection rule is based upon a common
sense observation of customer behavior : the typical
shopper does not retain all of the individual details
of a composite mark in his or her mind, but retains
only an overall, general impression created by the
composite as a whole. It is the overall impression
created by the mark from the ordinary shopper's
cursory observation in the marketplace that will or
will not lead to a likelihood of confusion, not the
impression created from a meticulous comparison
as expressed in carefully weighed analysis in legal
briefs. In litigation over the alleged similarity of
marks, the owner will emphasize the similarities
and the alleged infringer will emphasize the
differences. The point is that the two marks should
not be examined with a microscope to find the
differences, for this is not the way the average
purchaser views the marks. To the average buyer,
the points of similarity are more important that
minor points of difference. A court should not
engage in "technical gymnastics" in an attempt to
find some minor differences between conflicting
marks.
However, where there are both similarities
and differences in the marks, there must be
weighed against one another to see which
predominate.
The rationale of the anti-dissection rule is
based upon this assumption:"An average purchaser

6
does not retain all the details of a mark, but rather
the mental impression of the mark creates in its
totality. It has been held to be a violation of the
anti-dissection rule to focus upon the "prominent"
feature of a mark and decide likely confusion solely
upon that feature, ignoring all other elements of the
mark. Similarly, it is improper to find that one
portion of a composite mark has no trademark
significance, leading to a direct comparison between
only that which remains.""
10. Learned Senior Counsel submits that the registered trade
mark of the appellant and the trademark by which name the
respondent is running her business, are deceptively similar. It is
argued that it has to be seen from the perspective of a common
purchaser, who may come into the trap of deception. In this regard,
learned Senior Counsel has placed reliance on the principle of law
as laid down in the case of Amritdhara Pharmacy Vs. Satya Deo
Gupta, AIR 1963 SC 449.
11. In the case of Amritdhara Pharmacy (Supra), the
Hon'ble Supreme Court interpreted that word "likely to deceive or
cause confusion" and in para 6 observed as follows:-
"6. It will be noticed that the words used in
the sections and relevant for our purpose are "likely
to deceive or cause confusion". The Act does not lay
down any criteria for determining what is likely to
deceive or cause confusion. Therefore, every case
must depend on its own particular facts, and the
value of authorities lies not so much in the actual
decision as in the tests applied for determining
what is likely to deceive or cause confusion. On an
application to register, the Registrar or an opponent
may object that the trade mark is not registrable by
reason of clause (a) of Section 8, or sub-section (I)
of Section 10, as in this case. In such a case the
onus is on the applicant to satisfy the Registrar that
the trade mark applied for is not likely to deceive or

7
cause confusion. In cases in which the tribunal
considers that there is doubt as to whether
deception is likely, the application should be
refused. A trade mark is likely to deceive or cause
confusion by its resemblance to another already on
the Register if it is likely to do so in the course of its
legitimate use in a market where the two marks are
assumed to be in use by traders in that market. In
considering the matter, all the circumstances of the
case must be considered. As was observed by
Parker, J., in Pianotist Co Application, (1906) 23
RPC 774 - which was also a case of the comparison
of two words.
"You must take the two words. You must
judge them, both by their look and by their
sound. You consider the goods to which they are
to be applied. You must consider the nature and
kind of customer who would be likely to buy
those goods. In fact you must consider all the
surrounding circumstances; and you must
further consider what is likely to happen if each
of those trade marks is used in a normal way as
a trade mark for the goods of the respective
owners of the marks." (p. 777)
For deceptive resemblance two important
questions are : (1) who are the persons whom the
resemblance must be likely to deceive or confuse,
and (2) what rules of comparison are to be adopted
in judging whether such resemblance exists. As to
confusion, it is perhaps an appropriate description
of the state of mind of a customer who, on seeing a
mark thinks that it differs from the mark on goods
which he has previously bought, but is doubtful
whether that impression is not due to imperfect
recollection. (See Kerly on Trade Marks, 8th
Edition, p. 400.)"
12. Further, in the case of Amritdhara Pharmacy (Supra),
in para 8, the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed, "...A critical
comparison of the two names may disclose some points of
difference, but an unwary purchaser of average intelligence and
imperfect recollection would be deceived by the overall

8
similarity of the two names having regard to the nature of the
medicine he is looking for with a somewhat vague recollection
that he had purchased a similar medicine on a previous
occasion with a similar name. The trade mark is the whole
thing-the whole word has to be considered..."
13. Learned Senior Counsel would further argue that the
infringement of the trade marks has to be examined keeping in view
the fact that both the trade marks/labels are not before a common
purchaser. A purchaser or a person dealing with the business of
the appellant and the respondent may not have the opportunity of
having both the trade marks/labels side by side. He would refer to
the principle of law as laid down in the case of Parle Products (P)
Ltd. Vs. J.P. and Co. Mysore, (1972)1 SCC 618, in which case, in
para 8, the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed as follows:-
"8. According to Karly's Law of Trade Marks
and Trade Names (9th Edn., para 838):
"Two marks, when placed side by
side, may exhibit many and various
differences, yet the main idea left on the
mind by both may be the same. A person
acquainted with one mark, and not having
the two side by side for comparison, might
well be deceived, if the goods were allowed to
be impressed with the second mark, into a
belief that he was dealing with goods which
bore the same mark as that with which he
was acquainted. Thus, for example, a mark
may represent a game of football; another
mark may show players in a different dress,
and in very different positions, and yet the
idea conveyed by each might be simply a
game of football. It would be too much to
expect that persons dealing with trade
marked goods, and relying, as they
frequently do, upon marks, should be able

9
to remember the exact details of the marks
upon the goods with which they are in the
habit of dealing. Marks are remembered
rather by general impressions or by some
significant detail than by any photographic
recollection of the whole. Moreover,
variations in detail might well be supposed
by customers to have been made by the
owners of the trade mark they are already
acquainted with for reasons of their own.""
14. Further, in the case of Parle Products (Supra), the
Hon'ble Supreme Court in para 9 observed as follows:-
"9. It is, therefore, clear that in order
to come to the conclusion whether one mark
is deceptively similar to another, the broad
and essential features of the two are to be
considered. They should not be placed side
by side to find out if there are any
differences in the design and if so, whether
they are of such character as to prevent one
design from being mistaken for the other.
.................................................................
..............................................................."
15. Learned Senior Counsel would submit that prima facie
it is established that the trademark/label which the respondent is
using is similar to the registered trademark of the appellant and the
goods and services covered by the registered trade mark/label of
the appellant and the goods and services provided by the
respondent are similar or identical. Hence, it is submitted that
prima facie case of infringement of registered trade mark/label is
made out. He submits that actual loss in such cases is not
necessary to be established. He submits that in order to stop
infringement it is sufficient that the act may likely to cause
confusion.

10
16. Learned counsel appearing for the respondent submits
that the impugned order is in accordance with law, which does not
warrant any interference. He also raised the following points in his
submissions:-
(i) Both the trade marks/labels are quite distinct, in
pronunciation, in spelling, in their presentation,
etc. "SWARNIKA" alone is not the trade
mark/label, it is "SWARNIKA Gems and Jewels",
which is distinct from "SUNAREKA".
(ii) The trade mark/label should be compared as a
whole along with logo and name and if it is so
compared, both the trade marks/labels are quite
different. The trade mark/label which the
respondent is using may not likely to cause any
confusion or deception, especially when one
cannot see them on the product to be sold.
17. Learned counsel for the respondent also submits that
the scope of appeal against rejection of an application under Order
39, Rules 1 and 2 of the Code is quite restricted. In an appeal, if
there are two views possible, the view adopted by the trial court has
to be respected.
18. In support of his contention, learned counsel placed
reliance on the principle of law as laid down by the Hon'ble
Supreme Court in the case of Ramakant Ambalal Choksi Vs. Harish
Ambalal Choksi and others, (2024)11 SCC 351, in which case, the

11
Hon'ble Supreme Court preferred the principle of law as laid down
in the case of Wander Ltd. Vs. Antox India (P) Ltd., 1990 Supp SCC
727 and Evans Vs. Bartlam, 1937 A.C. 473 and many other case
laws and in para 21 to 25 observed as follows:-
"21. With regard to (a), this Court held thus:
(Wander case [Wander Ltd. v. Antox India (P) Ltd.,
1990 Supp SCC 727] , SCC p. 733, para 14)
"14. ... In such appeals, the appellate
court will not interfere with the exercise of
discretion of the court of the first instance
and substitute its own discretion, except
where the discretion has been shown to
have been exercised arbitrarily or
capriciously or perversely, or where the
court had ignored the settled principles of
law regulating grant or refusal of
interlocutory injunctions. ... The appellate
court will not reassess the material and seek
to reach a conclusion different from the one
reached by the court below.... If the
discretion has been exercised by the trial
court reasonably and in a judicial manner
the fact that the appellate court would have
taken a different view may not justify
interference with the trial court's exercise of
discretion."
22. This Court, while arriving at the above
findings, relied on its earlier judgment in Printers
(Mysore) (P) Ltd. v. Pothan Joseph [Printers (Mysore)
(P) Ltd. v. Pothan Joseph, 1960 SCC OnLine SC 62] ,
wherein it was held thus: (Printers case [Printers
(Mysore) (P) Ltd. v. Pothan Joseph, 1960 SCC
OnLine SC 62] , SCC OnLine SC para 9)
"9. ... as has been observed by
Viscount Simon LC in Charles Osenton &
Co. v. Johnston [Charles Osenton & Co. v.
Johnston, 1942 AC 130 (HL)] , the law as to
reversal by a court of appeal of an order
made by a Judge below in the exercise of
his/her discretion is well established, and
any difficulty that arises is due only to the

12
application of well-settled principles in an
individual case."
23. It is pertinent to note that in Printers
[Printers (Mysore) (P) Ltd. v. Pothan Joseph, 1960
SCC OnLine SC 62] this Court had held that
ignoring relevant facts is also a ground for
interfering with the discretion exercised by the trial
court. Furthermore, Viscount Simon LC in Charles
Osenton & Co. v. Johnston [Charles Osenton & Co. v.
Johnston, 1942 AC 130 (HL)] , after stating the
above, went on to quote Lord Wright's decision in
Evans v. Bartlam [Evans v. Bartlam, 1937 AC 473
(HL)] : (Evans case [Evans v. Bartlam, 1937 AC 473
(HL)] , AC p. 486)
"... It is clear that the court of appeal
should not interfere with the discretion of a
judge acting within his jurisdiction unless
the Court is clearly satisfied that he was
wrong. But the court is not entitled simply
to say that if the judge had jurisdiction and
had all the facts before him, the court of
appeal cannot review his order unless he is
shown to have applied a wrong principle.
The court must, if necessary, examine anew
the relevant facts and circumstances in
order to exercise a discretion by way of
review which may reverse or vary the order."
24. In Evans case [Evans v. Bartlam,
1937 AC 473 (HL)] , Lord Wright made it clear that
while adjudicating upon the discretion exercised by
the trial court, the appellate court is obliged to
consider the case put forward by the appellant in
favour of its argument that the trial court exercised
its discretion arbitrarily or incorrectly in the
circumstances.
25. What flows from a plain reading of
the decisions in Evans [Evans v. Bartlam, 1937 AC
473 (HL)] and Charles Osenton [Charles Osenton &
Co. v. Johnston, 1942 AC 130 (HL)] is that an
appellate court, even while deciding an appeal
against a discretionary order granting an interim
injunction, has to:

13
(a) Examine whether the discretion has
been properly exercised i.e. examine
whether the discretion exercised is
not arbitrary, capricious or contrary
to the principles of law; and
(b) In addition to the above, an appellate
court may in a given case have to
adjudicate on facts even in such
discretionary orders."
19. Reference has also been made to the judgment in the
case of Skyline Education Institute (India) Private Ltd. Vs. S.L.
Vaswani and another, (2010)2 SCC 142, with regard to power to be
exercised in appeal against an order rejecting a prayer for
injunction. In para 19 of the judgment, Hon'ble Supreme Court
observed as follows:-
"19. We have thoughtfully considered the
entire matter. Before pronouncing upon the
tenability or otherwise of the appellant's prayer for
restraining the respondents from using the word
"Skyline" for the Institute of Engineering and
Technology established by them, we consider it
necessary to observe that as the suit filed by the
appellant is pending trial and issues raised by the
parties are yet to be decided, the High Court rightly
considered and decided the appellant's prayer for
temporary injunction only on the basis of the
undisputed facts and the material placed before the
learned Single Judge and unless this Court comes
to the conclusion that the discretion exercised by
the High Court in refusing to entertain the
appellant's prayer for temporary injunction is
vitiated by an error apparent or perversity and
manifest injustice has been done to it, there will be
no warrant for exercise of power under Article 136
of the Constitution."
20. Learned counsel for the respondent also submits that the
matter has to be examined in entirety. At the stage of deciding of a

14
temporary injunction application, a mini trial may not be
conducted; the rights of the parties may not be determined finally;
the rights are decided finally after parties get an opportunity of
adducing evidences. He would submit that the prima facie case,
balance of convenience and irreparable loss have been examined by
the court below. The impugned order does not warrant any
interference and the best course in such situation would be to
maintain status quo. He would refer to the principle of law as laid
down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Maharwal
Khewaji Trust (Regd.) Vs. Baldev Dass, (2004) 8 SCC 488. In the
case of Maharwal Khewaji Trust (Regd.), the Hon'ble Supreme Court
accepted the argument that, "unless and until a case of
irreparable loss or damage is made out by a party to the suit,
the court should not permit the nature of the property being
changed which also includes alienation or transfer of the
property which may lead to loss or damage being caused to the
party who may ultimately succeed and may further lead to
multiplicity of proceedings."
21. Undoubtedly, in an order rejecting an application for
temporary injunction, it is not easily interfered with unless there
are valid reasons to do so. This relief basically rests on discretion
guided by the principle of law pronounced by the courts. The broad
and significant parameters are prima facie case, balance of
convenience and irreparable loss.
22. It is the case of the appellant that the registered
trademark/label is being infringed.

15
23. Section 29 of the Act is as follows:-
"29. Infringement of registered trade marks.-(1) A
registered trade mark is infringed by a person who, not being a
registered proprietor or a person using by way of permitted use, uses
in the course of trade, a mark which is identical with, or deceptively
similar to, the trade mark in relation to goods or services in respect of
which the trade mark is registered and in such manner as to render
the use of the mark likely to be taken as being used as a trade mark.
(2) A registered trade mark is infringed by a person who,
not being a registered proprietor or a person using by way of
permitted use, uses in the course of trade, a mark which because of-
(a) its identity with the registered trade mark
and the similarity of the goods or services
covered by such registered trade mark; or
(b) its similarity to the registered trade mark
and the identity or similarity of the goods or
services covered by such registered trade
mark; or
(c) its identity with the registered trade mark
and the identity of the goods or services
covered by such registered trade mark,
is likely to cause confusion on the part of the public, or which is
likely to have an association with the registered trade mark.
(3) In any case falling under clause (c) of sub-section (2),
the court shall presume that it is likely to cause confusion on the
part of the public.
(4) A registered trade mark is infringed by a person who,
not being a registered proprietor or a person using by way of
permitted use, uses in the course of trade, a mark which-
(a) is identical with or similar to the registered trade
mark; and
(b) is used in relation to goods or services which are
not similar to those for which the trade mark is
registered; and
(c) the registered trade mark has a reputation in India
and the use of the mark without due cause takes
unfair advantage of or is detrimental to, the
distinctive character or repute of the registered
trade mark.

16
(5) A registered trade mark is infringed by a person if he
uses such registered trade mark, as his trade name or part of his
trade name, or name of his business concern or part of the name, of
his business concern dealing in goods or services in respect of which
the trade mark is registered.
(6) For the purposes of this section, a person uses a
registered mark, if, in particular, he-
(a) affixes it to goods or the packaging thereof;
(b) offers or exposes goods for sale, puts them on the
market, or stocks them for those purposes under
the registered trade mark, or offers or supplies
services under the registered trade mark;
(c) imports or exports goods under the mark; or
(d) uses the registered trade mark on business papers
or in advertising.
(7) A registered trade mark is infringed by a person who
applies such registered trade mark to a material intended to be used
for labelling or packaging goods, as a business paper, or for
advertising goods or services, provided such person, when he applied
the mark, knew or had reason to believe that the application of the
mark was not duly authorised by the proprietor or a licensee.
(8) A registered trade mark is infringed by any advertising
of that trade mark if such advertising-
(a) takes unfair advantage of and is contrary to honest
practices in industrial or commercial matters; or
(b) is detrimental to its distinctive character; or
(c) is against the reputation of the trade mark.
(9) Where the distinctive elements of a registered trade
mark consist of or include words, the trade mark may be infringed by
the spoken use of those words as well as by their visual
representation and reference in this section to the use of a mark shall
be construed accordingly."
24. Trade mark in a business is a kind of lifeline. A business
runs through it. Its infringement gives right to its owner to bring a
suit to seek injunction.

17
25. In the case of Ramakant Ambalal Choksi (supra), the
Hon'ble Supreme Court based on the judgment in the case of Evans
(Supra) and Charles Osentons & Co. Vs. Johnston, 1942 A.C. 130
summed up the principle in para 25. At the cost of repetition, para
25 of the judgment in the case of Ramakant Ambalal Choksi (supra)
is being reproduced here once again:-
"25. What flows from a plain reading of the
decisions in Evans [Evans v. Bartlam, 1937 AC 473 (HL)]
and Charles Osenton [Charles Osenton & Co. v. Johnston,
1942 AC 130 (HL)] is that an appellate court, even while
deciding an appeal against a discretionary order granting
an interim injunction, has to:
(a) Examine whether the discretion has been
properly exercised i.e. examine whether the
discretion exercised is not arbitrary,
capricious or contrary to the principles of
law; and
(b) In addition to the above, an appellate court
may in a given case have to adjudicate on
facts even in such discretionary orders."
26. A bare reading of the aforesaid principles, makes it
abundantly clear that interference in the discretion exercised by the
trial court may not be made unless the discretion exercised is
arbitrary, capricious or contrary to the principles of law, and, in
some cases, the court may adjudicate on facts even in such
discretionary orders, if the order is wrong.
27. Learned counsel for both the parties have argued that
trademark/label has to be seen as a whole. Anti-dissection is a
rule; the words and letters cannot be read in isolation or in groups
or in disjunction. In the impugned order, the court has, in fact, did
dissection to both the words, "SUNAREKA" and "SWARNIKA",

18
which it appears is not permissible at this stage. The impugned
order also takes note of spelling.
28. It is also true that a person who comes across to the
business of the parties may not have the option of keeping both the
trademarks/labels side by side. As held in the case of Parle
Products (Supra), "A person acquainted with one mark, and not
having the two side by side for comparison, might well be
deceived, if the goods were allowed to be impressed with the
second mark, into a belief that he was dealing with goods
which bore the same mark as that with which he was
acquainted." Here is a case of deception or confusion and who are
the buyers, the general public in the city of Udham Singh Nagar.
29. As stated hereinbefore, the appellant did apply for his
trademark registration in the month of September, 2022 which was
granted to him on 28.07.2023. During the course of arguments,
learned Senior Counsel for the appellant referred to the reply notice
given by the respondent, particularly paras 2 and 3, which record
that the respondent has been doing wholesale business of
Gemstones, Rudraksha and Rudraksha Mala and sea pearls under
the trade name and style of "SHRI GURU RATAN KENDRA" since
2019 and in para 3 in the reply notice, it is written that recently
they started business of gold, jewelleries under the trade name and
style of "SWARNIKA JEWELLERY". This reply notice is dated
13.11.2023.
30. During the course of arguments, learned counsel
appearing for the respondent submits that in the month of June,

19
2023 the respondent started business in gold, jewelleries, as such.
It is argued that earlier when they were doing business with the
gemstones and sea pearls, there also they were using silver and
gold so as to cover those gemstones and pearls, etc.
31. So the chronology is clear. After the appellant's
application for registered trade mark in the month of September,
2022, some time in the month of June, 2023 respondent started
gold business. Earlier they were not into that business as such. On
28.07.2023, the appellant got his trademarks registered in the
name of "SUNAREKA". It is admitted at Bar that both the shops of
the appellant as well as of the respondent are in the same street
and at a distance of less than 500 Meters.
32. In the case of Amritdhara Pharmacy (Supra), the Hon'ble
Supreme Court had made a very critical analysis, then it was
observed that, "A critical comparison of the two names may
disclose some points of difference, but an unwary purchaser of
average intelligence and imperfect recollection would be
deceived by the overall similarity of the two names having
regard to the nature of the medicine................................."
Similar is the instant case. There is similarity in the marks which is
being used by the respondent. Their items are also similar.
Therefore, the appellant has, in fact, made out a prima facie case.
33. In so far as balance of convenience is concerned, it is the
case of the appellant that he has also been into the business of
jewelleries for the last approximately 12 years.

20
34. Learned counsel for the respondent submits that earlier
that in the year 1962 the respondent's business was in the name of
"Guru" Jewellers. The fact remains that in their reply notice dated
13.11.2023, the respondent has replied saying that recently they
started business of gold jewelleries under the name of
"Swarnika".
35. In view of the foregoing discussions, this Court is of the
view that, in fact, the balance of convenience also lies in favour of
the appellant.
36. In so far as irreparable loss is concerned, the business of
the appellant in the name of registered trademark is violated.
Definitely, it may cause irreparable loss to the appellant.
37. In view of the aforesaid, this Court is of the view that the
court below has committed an error in rejecting the application.
Consequently, the appeal deserves to be allowed.
38. The appeal is allowed.
39. The impugned order dated 18.07.2026, passed in Civil
Suit No.01 of 2024, Deepanshu Bansal Vs. Poonam Bhatt, by the
court of First Additional District Judge, Udham Singh Nagar is set
aside.
40. The application filed before the court below on behalf of
the appellant herein under Order 39 Rule 1 & 2 read with Section
151 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, is allowed. By way of ad-interim injunction, the respondent is restrained from
